new_statements.quote: 7. Stress is almost invariably penultimate in Muna. This is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed. Stress is therefore not marked.
new_statements.citation: van den Berg, Rene. 1991. Muna dialects and Munic languages: towards a reconstruction. In Ray Harlow (ed.), VICAL 2: Western Austronesian and contact languages. Papers from the Fifth International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, 21-51. Auckland: Linguistic Society of New Zealand.
new_statements.locator: p. 27, section 2 (notes on Muna phonology and transcription), point 7; Kaimbulawa identified as one of the languages 'to be discussed' at p. 24 ('On Siompu another language is also found, Kaimbulawa, to be discussed in 6') and sec. 6, pp. 44-45 (author's own wordlists for Kaimbulawa KAIM, Lantoi LANT, Kambe-Kambero KAMBE)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote: the page image (printed p. 27 = PDF p. 8 of, running head 'Muna Dialects and Munic Languages') shows sec. 2 point 7 exactly as reported: '7. Stress is almost invariably penultimate in Muna. This is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed. Stress is therefore not marked.' The scanned ( lines 287-289) matches. Context read: points 5-6 (open syllables, V/CV only; identical-vowel sequences heterosyllabic) precede it and sec. 3 'Muna dialects: phonological differences' follows, so point 7 closes the author's notes on Muna phonology/transcription that govern all forms cited in the paper. Identity: p. 24 (scanned l. 179) 'On Siompu another language is also found, Kaim…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable, near-exceptionlessly, in Muna and equally in the other Muna dialects and Munic (Pancanic) languages treated in the paper, among them Kaimbulawa, for which the author collected the wordlists himself; stress is therefore left unmarked in all cited forms.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'almost invariably'; no exceptions are listed for Kaimbulawa or any other isolect. (Van den Berg 2003:95-96 separately notes a Muna exception, 'nine' with antepenultimate stress after glide syllabification, and reconstructs Proto Muna-Buton stress as penultimate.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is a transcription convention covering isolated wordlist items (citation forms) for all isolects in the paper; it is a blanket areal/genetic statement extended from Muna to Kaimbulawa rather than a dedicated description of Kaimbulawa prosody. No Kaimbulawa-specific phonology exists in print.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is made for Muna and explicitly extended to 'the other dialects and languages to be discussed', which in this paper include Kaimbulawa (KAIM, village Kaimbulawa, SE tip of Siompu), its Lantoi dialect (LANT) and Kambe-Kambero (KAMBE, SW coast of Buton), i.e. exactly Glottolog kaim1241 / ISO zka, from the author's own wordlists. It is not a dedicated Kaimbulawa description. Note that Badan Bahasa's Peta Bahasa classes 'dialek Kaimbulawa' as a Wolio dialect by dialectometry, and that the Muna 'Siompu dialect' (desa Tongali) on the same island is a different variety (Muna, muna1247), not Kaimbulawa.

sources.note: p. 27, sec. 2 point 7: 'Stress is almost invariably penultimate in Muna. This is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed. Stress is therefore not marked.' Kaimbulawa (KAIM; with Lantoi LANT and Kambe-Kambero KAMBE) is one of the non-Muna speech communities whose wordlists the author collected himself and discusses in sec. 6 (pp. 44-45).
